nodes.label: Signatory feature (decisions document)
nodes.rationale: Running decision document. The design changed substantially on 27 August 2026: until then nobody had looked at a physical fuel document, and the assumption that a signatory is a person with a typed name and typed position title in a table of their own turned out to be untrue. Cost was one edit, because no signatory table had been built.

nodes.label: There is no signatory table
nodes.source_location: Where this stands / What no longer exists
nodes.rationale: On the real documents nobody's title is ever typed: it is printed on the form as a caption, or fixed and identical every time, or read from the person's own record. So no signatory row, no typed name, no typed position title and no signatory date range. A document points at a version of an employee instead.

nodes.label: Signature block
nodes.rationale: The whole printed block where somebody signs: its label such as Requested by, the name, and the title printed underneath. One settled word was chosen after 'signing line' had been used loosely, sometimes for the whole block and sometimes only for its label.

nodes.label: Caption (a title printed on the paper)
nodes.rationale: The test is not what the words look like but where they come from. 'GSU Representative' would sit under anybody's name, so it is a caption and nothing is stored; 'AO-I/Supply Officer' changes with the person, so it is their own title. The word 'designation' is deliberately not used, because in this project it means an extra role a person holds on a group. Roughly half the fuel signature blocks are captions, which removes a large part of the problem: there is no roster to keep and nothing that goes out of date.

nodes.label: Every signature block carries two rules, written in code
nodes.source_location: The design as it now stands
nodes.rationale: Who may be chosen (any employee, only a named unit's staff, only people able to do something, one particular post, or nobody) and where the printed title comes from (a caption on the form, or the person's own title as it was at the time). There is no third rule for a fixed string written into the program — the RIS approver is picked from a list and prints their own title; it only looks fixed because the same person is nearly always chosen.

nodes.label: A document stores a reference to an employee history row
nodes.rationale: One column per signature block, holding a history row id or nothing. Storing the name as text would freeze a typo permanently across every record that used it — the user's point being that nobody would remember which thirty records held a misspelled name. With versions, a spelling fix is an edit in place that corrects everything, and a marriage or promotion is a new version that leaves old documents alone. A per-report-type signatory table was rejected for the same reason: anybody signing two kinds of document would need the fix repeated in each.

nodes.label: A mistake and a real change need opposite behaviour
nodes.rationale: Editing a version means 'this was always wrong, correct it everywhere'; creating one means 'this changed from now on'. The wording offered to whoever does data entry became 'Fix a mistake in what was typed' and 'Record a change that happened' on 1 September 2026, because the same version row holds the position title and the older name-only wording read wrong for a promotion. The two-button screen described here was superseded: the employee document's Topic 10 replaced the question with two separate actions.

nodes.label: Config table (one row per setting)
nodes.source_location: How a signature block knows who may be chosen
nodes.rationale: A key that is a fixed string in the code and a plain text value the office fills in, so the code never hardcodes a row id that means nothing on another installation. Rejected alternatives: a short fixed code column on org_unit (an admin must populate it but may not edit it later, which is confusing), typed columns on the config table (columns only one row would ever use), and deriving the GSU unit from whoever first opens the page holding gsu:view (a permission belongs to a role, not to a unit, so the mistake would surface much later with no visible cause). Not built yet — it waits for the fuel work.

nodes.label: Protecting a config reference in code, not by foreign key
nodes.source_location: How a signature block knows who may be chosen
nodes.rationale: A foreign key with restrict would only have protected deletion, while deactivating an org unit is an ordinary column change no foreign key can catch, so the check was needed anyway. One mechanism covering both beats two covering one each. Accepted cost: it holds only while every path goes through a single delete-and-deactivate function with the check inside it, rather than the check being copied into each screen.

nodes.label: fuel.gsu_org_unit setting
nodes.source_location: How a signature block knows who may be chosen
nodes.rationale: Names the General Services Unit so blocks restricted to GSU staff can be filled from employee.org_unit_fk. There is only one GSU and any of its staff may approve any section's slip, so an earlier sketch giving the roster its own org unit was dropped — different names on the GSU and CDS copies were simply who happened to sign.

nodes.label: fuel.penr_officer default approver setting
nodes.source_location: How a signature block knows who may be chosen
nodes.rationale: Holds an employee id used only as the default choice. No warning is raised when that person is marked separated: the value is cleared next time it is read, the approver comes up empty, the RIS will not save, and the requester walks to GSU and asks who approves now — which is how the office already works and puts the question in front of the people who know the answer. The real failure case is separation rather than deletion, since the database already refuses to delete an employee anything links to.

nodes.label: Every block gets a default, and defaults are checked before use
nodes.source_location: Every signature block gets a default
nodes.rationale: The user's own condition, to remove the awkward case of a line with nobody suggested. Somebody no longer working is never filled in, never appears in the selection list so they cannot be picked by hand, and a document will not save naming them, whether they arrived as a default or were chosen deliberately.

nodes.label: The list is built from the document's filed date
nodes.source_location: The list is built from the document's filed date
nodes.rationale: The user's design, and the mechanism the other rules fall out of. The form asks who was valid on the paper's date, comparing against valid_from and valid_until, not who is working today. A slip filed last month still offers last month's people so it can be reprinted and signed per procurationem; a slip filed today does not; editing an old document needs no special case. This is why marking somebody as no longer working must also close their open history row, not only change a status.

nodes.label: Signing happens on paper only
nodes.rationale: Confirmed with the supervisor and again on the physical documents. The system prepares and prints documents with the correct names; no signatory logs in to approve and no signed-on date is stored. An earlier answer saying signing happened both on paper and in the system had created a problem that no longer exists — signers without an account could never approve, so 'not signed yet' and 'will never be signed here' were indistinguishable.

nodes.label: A signature block may be printed blank
nodes.rationale: Confirmed on paper: the Withdrawal Slip's supplier block is always blank, and the CDS copy of the RIS has an empty Received by left for a hand to fill in. So a report is not incomplete merely because a block has nobody attached, and 'no signatory available for a block' stopped being a conflict worth checking.

nodes.label: Per procurationem signing
nodes.rationale: Signing on somebody else's behalf with their authority, observed four times on the CDS copies. Invisible to the system: the printed name never changes and everything the substitute adds — initials, a handwritten name, a title such as 'OIC, Chief TSD / In-charge, Office of the PENR Officer' — is written with a pen after printing, anywhere near the block.

nodes.label: OIC — two different things at this office
nodes.rationale: There is no actual PENR Officer; Nathaniel E. Rancho has been OIC for years and every fuel document prints 'OIC, PENR Officer'. Temporary cover while he is away is also called OIC but never reaches the system, being handwritten. Nothing to build for either sense. An earlier version said an OIC was another signatory row with the acting title typed in, which was wrong twice over: no signatory rows exist, and the acting title is handwritten.

nodes.label: Signature blocks are fixed in code, one column each
nodes.rationale: Letting an admin add blocks from a screen would let them break the layout of the printed page, which the office does not want to be possible. With one column per block the line is the column name, so no label column and no admin-editable table of signing-line types. Accepted consequence: adding, removing or renaming a block is a developer change.

nodes.label: The same person may fill two blocks of one document
nodes.rationale: Allowed with no warning. Real case: a GSU staff member requesting fuel for a GSU vehicle qualifies for both Requested by and Approved by. The user watched an office head approve their own leave application when the admin officer was away, which is a stronger argument than the written rule. The rule belongs to the form, not to the employee data — nothing about a person makes them ineligible.

nodes.label: Choosing the wrong person is not the system's problem
nodes.source_location: Choosing the wrong person is not the system's problem
nodes.rationale: The system's job is to stop what is impossible, such as naming somebody who no longer works at the agency. Deciding who ought to sign is the office's job: GSU simply refuses to sign a slip naming the wrong person, and it is printed again. The control is social rather than technical, and it keeps the design small.

nodes.label: A fuel report is three documents printed together
nodes.rationale: Withdrawal Slip, Driver Trip Ticket and Requisition and Issue Slip, with different blocks, different rules and different numbers of blocks. Topic 5 had assumed one form per report; the decision survived and now applies per document.

nodes.label: Withdrawal Slip
nodes.rationale: Three blocks, not two: Requested by (any employee, caption 'Section Incharge'), Approved by (GSU personnel only, caption 'GSU Representative'), and the supplier's block, where nobody may be chosen because the gasoline station owner is not in the system and signs by hand.

nodes.label: Driver Trip Ticket
nodes.rationale: Approved by the PENR Officer or whoever is OIC, printing the officer's own title; and 'I hereby certify in accordance of the statement of travel', open to any employee who can drive including staff whose job has nothing to do with driving, always printing the caption 'Driver'.

nodes.label: Requisition and Issue Slip (RIS)
nodes.rationale: The document that actually prints people's own position titles, which is why it needs employee history at all. Four blocks: Requested by (defaulting to whoever is entering the report), Approved by (defaulted to the usual approver), Issued by (GSU only, with a usual default) and Received by, which may be left blank.

nodes.label: Working group titles are captions
nodes.rationale: Settled by the user and it needs no mechanism at all: a title on a Technical Working Group, an association or the BAC Secretariat is printed on the paper, and such titles appear on particular documents like memoranda rather than on these fill-in forms. Deliberately not designed earlier, because everything designed from conversation alone during this discussion turned out wrong once real paper appeared, and nothing was blocked by waiting. This is also what killed the coined terms 'position signatory' and 'designation signatory'.

nodes.label: One person has exactly one short form
nodes.source_location: Employee history, and who is accountable
nodes.rationale: Asked whether the same person ever prints different short forms on different documents, the user answered that it happens only because whoever typed it did not know the correct one — a mistake rather than a real difference. So the system holds one short form per person and uses it everywhere, which is also why it belongs on the employee rather than on a per-document record.

nodes.label: Record every employee, not only system users
nodes.rationale: Option 1, full separation, chosen over employees-only-for-non-users (the office's people would then live in two different tables) and over letting user be the employee table (the login code would become responsible for always excluding password-less rows, which is easy to get wrong later). It closed the gap that some signatories never log in, and an employee list is useful on its own.

nodes.label: Five things ruled out of a signature block
nodes.rationale: The other five report areas were closed on 31 August 2026 without holding the paper, by asking one narrow question answerable from experience. Ruled out: a group title typed under a name (it belongs to the seat and outlives whoever fills it, so it is printed), a block taking several names (what happens instead is several blocks sharing a caption, so nothing should be keyed on captions), a name that is not an employee, a professional licence number (such reports are written in a word processor instead), and a date inside the block (real on 40 to 50 percent of forms but always handwritten). What would reopen it: finding something printed inside a block that is none of the three allowed things; the licence number stays the worked example of the harder case, where the new fact is about the person rather than the form.
